title: Antoinette Handy and the NEA jazz panel
summary: Discussion of Handy, her sister Geneva Southall and Marsalis's four years on the NEA panel.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Being honored: NEA Jazz Masters and other awards

blocks.x: a classical flautist. She wrote a book on – her mentor was – what’s this woman’s name? She wrote this book on African-American music.

Yeah. Her mentor was Eileen Southern. She wrote one book on black composers and another one – I can’t remember what the other one was. The third one, she passed, and her daughter told me that she was going to get the book out, but I don’t know if she ever did or not. Anyway, I recommended her. She in turn asked me to be on the jazz panel. I spent four years on that panel.
Yeah. Antoinette Handy-Miller. I spent four years on that panel. I wasn’t supposed to do that, because I think it was a three-year thing, max.
I wonder if she was – I think she might have studied with Geneva Southall. Is that right? Or did she study with Eileen Southern? But that’s okay. I’ll check that.
I’m just trying to figure out – you mentioned about the woman who wrote the history of African-American music. I know Eileen Southern. I know Geneva Southall was also – but anyway . . .
Geneva Southall wrote the book on Blind Tom. Geneva Southall was Antoinette’s sister.
That’s it. I knew there was a connection. That’s it. Thank you.
And that was my first piano teacher.
